sections.title: Dataset Engineering
sections.sub: Curating, synthesizing, and processing the data that decides how good your finetuned model can be

bn.title: ডেটাসেট ইঞ্জিনিয়ারিং
bn.sub: ফাইন-টিউন করা মডেলের মান যে ডেটার ওপর নির্ভর করে, সেই ডেটা কিউরেট, সিন্থেসাইজ আর প্রসেস করার পদ্ধতি

body.html: Why dataset engineering matters

No amount of compute or model skill can fix bad data. The goal of dataset engineering is to build a dataset that lets you train the best model you can within your budget. As fewer teams build foundation models from scratch, data has become the main place where teams can still differentiate their model's performance, which is why many AI companies now have dedicated data labelers, dataset creators, and data quality engineers.

blocks.html: Data-centric vs. model-centric AI: model-centric AI improves results by changing the model (architecture, size, training technique). Data-centric AI keeps the model fixed and improves results by improving the data. In practice, strong progress usually needs investment in both.

body.html: Different training phases need different kinds of data. Pre-training mostly needs raw sequences at huge token counts. Instruction finetuning needs (instruction, response) pairs. Preference finetuning needs (instruction, winning response, losing response) triples, or scored responses for reward modeling. Across all phases, though, the same three questions decide whether a dataset is good: is it high quality, does it have good coverage, and is there enough of it?
Data quality

A small amount of high-quality data regularly beats a large amount of noisy data. Studies on models like Yi and LIMA found that a few thousand carefully written examples can match or beat results from hundreds of thousands of messy ones. Quality is normally judged on six properties: data should be relevant to the task, aligned with what the task actually needs (not just technically correct), consistent across examples and annotators, correctly formatted with no stray tokens or markup, sufficiently unique so duplicates don't bias training, and compliant with privacy and licensing rules.

items: Relevant: the example should match the task's domain and time period.
Aligned: annotations should match what the task actually rewards, e.g. creativity for a creative task, conciseness for a concise one.
Consistent: two annotators scoring the same example should agree; this needs clear annotation guidelines.
Correctly formatted: no leftover HTML, inconsistent casing, or trailing whitespace.
Sufficiently unique: duplicate examples can introduce bias and leak into the test set.
Compliant: no data you aren't legally or contractually allowed to use, such as PII.

body.html: Data coverage and data quantity

Coverage (often called data diversity) means your training data spans the range of inputs your model will actually see in production — different phrasing styles, topics, output formats, and languages. What diversity matters depends on the application: a translation tool mostly needs stylistic diversity, while a general-purpose chatbot needs diversity in topic, task type, and tone.

rows: Instruction style, task type, length diversity
Coverage of the real distribution of user preferences

body.html: There is no universal answer to "how much data do I need." More examples generally help, but returns diminish quickly: the first thousand examples might move accuracy by ten points, the next thousand by five. A practical approach is to finetune on subsets of your current data (25%, 50%, 100%) and plot a performance-vs-size curve: a steep slope means more data will keep helping, a flat one means you're near the ceiling. Besides quality and coverage, three things change how much data you need: the finetuning technique (full finetuning needs far more data than LoRA-style PEFT), task complexity, and how strong your base model already is.
Data augmentation and synthesis

Data augmentation creates new examples from real data you already have (e.g., flipping an image, swapping a word for a synonym). Data synthesis creates data that mimics real data without being derived from a specific real example (e.g., a simulated API response). People reach for synthetic data to increase quantity, improve coverage of rare or sensitive cases, improve quality (AI can sometimes write more consistent preference labels than humans), protect privacy, and to distill a smaller model from a larger one.

items: Rule-based and template synthesis: fill a template (an invoice, a transaction record) with randomly generated values — fast and safe for sensitive formats like financial data.
Perturbation: add small amounts of noise or word swaps to existing data to create new, slightly harder examples and build robustness.

Simulation: generate data inside a virtual environment instead of the real world — common for self-driving cars, robotics, and tool-use agents, where real data collection is slow, costly, or dangerous.
AI-powered synthesis: use a foundation model to paraphrase, translate, generate instructions, generate responses, or play both sides of a conversation (self-play).

body.html: AI-powered instruction data synthesis usually starts from a small seed set (as in Self-Instruct and Alpaca), then asks a strong model to generate many more instructions and responses that mirror the seed examples in style and difficulty. A useful variant is reverse instruction: start from high-quality existing text (a book chapter, a Wikipedia article) and ask the model to generate the instruction that would have produced it — this sidesteps the fact that models are better at writing short instructions than long, accurate responses.

blocks.html: Synthetic data is not free of risk. Three documented failure modes are: superficial imitation (the student model copies the teacher's style without its underlying ability, which can push the student to hallucinate confidently), model collapse (training recursively on AI-generated data degrades a model over generations, as rare patterns slowly disappear), and obscured data lineage (if the generator model saw copyrighted or contaminated benchmark data, that risk and bias can silently flow into your model).

body.html: Because of these risks, generated data still needs verification: functional checks when possible (does the generated code pass its tests?), an AI judge or scorer otherwise, and simple heuristics such as filtering out examples that are too short, too repetitive, or where the instruction and response barely differ from other pairs in the set.
Model distillation

Model distillation trains a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher model, usually by training the student on data the teacher generated. The classic motivation is deployment cost: DistilBERT keeps 97% of BERT's language understanding at 40% of the size and 60% of the latency. Alpaca is a well-known instruction-tuning example — a 7-billion-parameter Llama finetuned on outputs from a 175-billion-parameter model. Not every model can be legally distilled: many providers' terms of service forbid using their outputs to train a competing model.
Data processing: inspect, deduplicate, clean, format

Once data is gathered (real or synthetic), it still has to be processed before it is training-ready. The four recurring steps are inspection, deduplication, cleaning/filtering, and formatting — in whichever order saves the most compute, since there's no fixed sequence that always wins.

blocks.html: Look at token/length distributions, topic and language mix, and manually read a sample of examples. Manual inspection repeatedly catches problems automated statistics miss.

Remove exact and near-duplicate examples using pairwise similarity, hashing (MinHash, Bloom filters), or dimensionality reduction first. Duplicates can bias the model and leak between train and test sets — one study showed repeating just 0.1% of data 100 times degraded an 800M-parameter model to the performance of a 400M-parameter one.

Strip stray formatting (HTML/Markdown), remove anything non-compliant (PII, copyrighted, toxic content), and remove low-quality examples using the same verification techniques used for synthetic data.

Convert data into the exact chat template and (instruction, response) structure your target model expects. A mismatched format at inference time — a missing arrow, an extra space, an added prefix — can silently break a finetuned model's behavior.

layman.html: Think of training a model like cooking. The data you feed it is the ingredients. Data quality is whether the ingredients are fresh and good. Data coverage is whether you have the right mix of ingredients, not just lots of one thing. Data quantity is simply how much food you're making.

blocks.html: The student analogy: giving a model messy, inconsistent training data is like teaching a new employee from confusing, contradictory examples of "good work." They will confidently learn the wrong habits. A handful of excellent, consistent examples teaches faster and better than a mountain of mixed-quality ones.

layman.html: Since getting enough high-quality human-written data is hard and expensive, teams increasingly use AI to generate more training data — this is called data synthesis. It's powerful, but risky if left unchecked: if you keep training new models only on data made by older AI models, quality can slowly drift and degrade over time, a problem researchers call model collapse. That's why generated data still needs checking before it's trusted.

items: Good data beats more data, almost every time.
AI can help create more data, but someone (or something) still has to check that it's actually good.
Before training, raw data usually needs cleanup: removing duplicates, stripping junk formatting, and putting it in the exact shape the model expects.

bangla.html: মডেলের performance সরাসরি নির্ভর করে তার training data-র ওপর। যত ভালো compute আর যত ভালো engineer থাকুক না কেন, ডেটা খারাপ হলে ভালো ফাইন-টিউন করা মডেল পাওয়া যায় না। তাই এখন অনেক AI কোম্পানিতে আলাদা করে data labeler, dataset creator, আর data quality engineer থাকেন।

ডেটা মূল্যায়ন করার তিনটি মূল মাপকাঠি হলো data quality (ডেটা কতটা নির্ভুল আর সামঞ্জস্যপূর্ণ), data coverage বা diversity (ডেটায় বাস্তব ব্যবহারের সব ধরনের বৈচিত্র্য আছে কিনা), আর data quantity (পরিমাণে পর্যাপ্ত কিনা)। গবেষণায় বারবার দেখা গেছে, অল্প কিন্তু উচ্চমানের ডেটা অনেক সময় বিশাল পরিমাণ noisy ডেটার চেয়ে ভালো ফল দেয়।

blocks.html: রান্নার উপমা: training data হলো উপকরণ। quality মানে উপকরণ তাজা কিনা, coverage মানে উপকরণের মিশ্রণ ঠিক আছে কিনা (বেশি বা কম চিনি না), আর quantity মানে কতটা রান্না করছেন।

bangla.html: যথেষ্ট পরিমাণে human-annotated ডেটা পাওয়া কঠিন ও ব্যয়বহুল বলে, এখন অনেক টিম data synthesis-এর দিকে ঝুঁকছে — অর্থাৎ একটি foundation model ব্যবহার করে নতুন instruction আর response তৈরি করা। এমনকি model distillation-ও এক ধরনের synthesis, যেখানে একটি ছোট student model একটি বড় teacher model-এর তৈরি করা আউটপুট দেখে শেখে, যেমন Alpaca মডেলটি GPT-3-এর একটি সংস্করণের আউটপুট দিয়ে ফাইন-টিউন করা হয়েছিল।

blocks.html: তবে সতর্ক থাকতে হবে: synthetic data নিয়ে কাজ করলে model collapse-এর ঝুঁকি আছে — বারবার AI-generated ডেটা দিয়ে ট্রেনিং করলে মডেলের মান ধীরে ধীরে খারাপ হতে পারে। তাই generated ডেটা সবসময় যাচাই (verify) করে নিতে হবে।

bangla.html: ডেটা সংগ্রহ করার পর সরাসরি ট্রেনিংয়ে ব্যবহার করা যায় না। এর আগে চারটি ধাপ লাগে: ডেটা inspect করা (দেখে বোঝা কী আছে), deduplicate করা (একই ডেটা বারবার থাকলে বায়াস তৈরি হয়), clean ও filter করা (নোংরা formatting আর নিম্নমানের উদাহরণ সরানো), আর শেষে মডেলের চাহিদা অনুযায়ী সঠিক ফরম্যাটে সাজানো।

sections.title: Inference Optimization
sections.sub: Making a trained model fast and cheap to run in production

bn.title: ইনফারেন্স অপ্টিমাইজেশন
bn.sub: ট্রেইন করা মডেলকে প্রোডাকশনে দ্রুত আর সস্তায় চালানো

body.html: Why inference optimization matters

Training builds a model; inference is using that model to answer real requests. Once a model ships, its usability depends less on raw quality and more on whether it responds fast enough and cheaply enough. The component that runs a model in production is the inference server, and the broader system around it (routing, queuing, preprocessing) is the inference service.

Optimization can target three levels: the model (make the model itself smaller or more efficient), the hardware (build or pick better chips), and the service (manage requests and resources better). These levels interact, and most production systems combine techniques from more than one.
Compute-bound vs. memory bandwidth-bound

Every workload hits one of two bottlenecks. A compute-bound task is limited by how many calculations the hardware can do; a memory bandwidth-bound task is limited by how fast data can move between memory and processors. For autoregressive language models, prefill (processing the input prompt in parallel) is compute-bound, while decode (generating one output token at a time) is memory bandwidth-bound, because each step must reload the model's weights to produce a single token.

items: Compute-bound workloads speed up with chips that have more raw FLOP/s.
Memory bandwidth-bound workloads speed up with chips that have higher memory bandwidth.
Because decode dominates response time for long outputs, many LLM-serving optimizations focus on the memory bandwidth-bound side.

body.html: Key performance metrics
Three numbers describe an inference service: latency (user experience), throughput (how much the service produces, tied to cost), and utilization (how efficiently hardware is used).

rows: How long until the first token appears; driven by the prefill step and input length.
How quickly each subsequent token is generated; driven by decode.
Roughly TTFT + TPOT × number of output tokens.
Output tokens per second across all requests; directly tied to compute cost.
Requests per second that meet a latency target (SLO), not just requests completed.
Model FLOP/s Utilization and Model Bandwidth Utilization: how close actual throughput gets to a chip's theoretical peak.

blocks.html: Latency is a distribution, not a single number. A few slow outlier requests can badly skew an average, so teams report percentiles such as p50, p90, p95, and p99 instead.

body.html: AI accelerators

An accelerator is a chip built for one kind of workload. GPUs dominate AI because, unlike CPUs (a few powerful general-purpose cores), they pack thousands of smaller cores suited to the massively parallel matrix multiplications behind most ML workloads. Other accelerators — Google's TPU, AWS Inferentia, Intel's Gaudi, and more — target training, inference, or edge devices specifically.

Three specs matter most when evaluating a chip: computational capability (FLOP/s, which drops as numeric precision increases), memory size and bandwidth (CPU DRAM is cheapest and slowest, GPU high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, is faster, and on-chip SRAM is fastest but tiny), and power consumption (maximum power draw and TDP). Quantization reduces how many bytes per parameter a model needs, which directly reduces the memory bandwidth it consumes.
Model-level optimization

Model optimization changes the model to make it cheaper to run, which can also change its output quality. Transformer-based language models are expensive mainly because of three traits: model size, autoregressive decoding, and the attention mechanism.

items: Model compression: quantization (lower-precision weights) and distillation (train a small model to mimic a large one) shrink a model's footprint. Pruning removes or zeroes out the least useful parameters, making the model sparser, though it is harder to apply well and less common in practice.

Speculative decoding: a small, fast draft model proposes several tokens, and the large target model verifies them all in one parallel pass, accepting the longest correct prefix. This turns part of decode's sequential cost into a parallel, compute-bound check.
Inference with reference: when a response is likely to reuse chunks of the input (quoting a document, editing code), those spans are copied directly instead of regenerated token by token.
Parallel decoding (e.g., Medusa, lookahead decoding): multiple candidate future tokens are generated at once and verified together, breaking the one-token-at-a-time dependency.

Attention and KV cache optimization: the KV cache stores previously computed key/value vectors so they are not recomputed at every step, but it grows with sequence length and batch size and can dominate memory use. Techniques include redesigning attention (local windowed attention, multi-query attention, grouped-query attention, cross-layer attention), smarter KV cache management (e.g., vLLM's PagedAttention), and hand-written kernels such as FlashAttention that fuse several operations into one fast pass.

body.html: Kernels and compilers

A kernel is hardware-specific code written for a repeated, performance-critical operation, such as matrix multiplication or attention. Common kernel-writing techniques include vectorization, parallelization, loop tiling, and operator fusion. A compiler (such as torch.compile, XLA, or TensorRT) lowers a general model script into kernels optimized for the target chip, bridging model code and hardware.
Inference service optimization
Service-level techniques manage a fixed pool of compute and memory across many simultaneous requests without touching the model's output quality.

items: Batching: grouping multiple requests together to use hardware more efficiently. Static batching waits for a full batch before running (simple but can delay early requests). Dynamic batching runs when the batch is full or a time window expires, whichever comes first. Continuous (in-flight) batching returns each response the moment it finishes and immediately slots in a new request, avoiding wasted capacity.
Decoupling prefill and decode: since the two steps have opposite bottlenecks, running them on separate machines avoids them competing for the same resources and improves both TTFT and TPOT.
Prompt caching: overlapping text across requests (like a shared system prompt or a long reference document) is processed once and reused, cutting both latency and cost for repeated context.

Parallelism strategies: replica parallelism runs multiple full copies of a model to serve more requests; tensor parallelism splits individual operators (like a matrix multiply) across devices to fit and speed up large models; pipeline parallelism splits a model into stages across devices, which raises per-request latency but helps throughput, so it is more common in training than in latency-sensitive inference; context and sequence parallelism split long inputs or their operators across machines.

blocks.html: Most optimization techniques are meant to leave model quality unchanged, but in practice many can shift it slightly. Comparing an inference provider's cost and speed without also checking output quality can be misleading.

layman.html: Once a model is trained, someone still has to run it for real users, and that costs money and takes time for every single response. This chapter is about making that running step — called inference — faster and cheaper without ruining the model's answers.

Two things slow a model down: generating the very first word of a reply (waiting time) and generating each word after that (typing speed). Engineers measure both separately, because an application can feel instant on one and sluggish on the other.

blocks.html: Restaurant kitchen analogy: reading an order and gathering ingredients is like prefill — it can be done quickly by many hands at once. Cooking the dish step by step is like decode — it happens one step after another and cannot be rushed past a point. A busy kitchen that groups similar orders together (batching), reuses prepped ingredients across orders (caching), and lets fast hands assist the chef (speculative decoding) serves far more diners without making anyone wait longer.

items: Shrinking the model (quantization, distillation, pruning) makes it lighter and faster to run.
Clever tricks like having a small helper model draft guesses, or reusing repeated text, can speed up word-by-word generation.
Serving many users at once (batching), splitting a model across multiple machines, and caching reused text are all ways to serve more people with the same hardware.

layman.html: None of this changes what the model knows — it only changes how quickly and cheaply it delivers what it already knows.

bangla.html: একটা মডেল ট্রেইন করার পর, আসল চ্যালেঞ্জ হলো সেটাকে প্রোডাকশনে চালানো — একে বলে inference। মডেল যত ভালোই হোক, যদি রেসপন্স আসতে অনেক সময় লাগে বা খরচ বেশি পড়ে, তাহলে সেটা ইউজারের জন্য কাজে লাগে না।
অটোরিগ্রেসিভ ল্যাঙ্গুয়েজ মডেলের ইনফারেন্স দুইটা ধাপে হয়: prefill (ইনপুট টোকেনগুলো একসাথে প্রসেস করা, যা compute-bound) আর decode (একটা একটা করে আউটপুট টোকেন জেনারেট করা, যা memory bandwidth-bound)।

items: TTFT (Time to First Token) মাপে প্রথম টোকেন আসতে কত সময় লাগে।
TPOT (Time Per Output Token) মাপে প্রতিটা পরের টোকেন কত দ্রুত আসে।
Throughput আর goodput বলে দেয় সার্ভিস কতটা দ্রুত এবং কতজন ইউজারের SLO পূরণ করে।

bangla.html: মডেল লেভেলে অপ্টিমাইজেশনের জন্য আছে quantization, distillation, pruning এর মতো model compression টেকনিক, আর speculative decoding-এর মতো পদ্ধতি, যেখানে একটা ছোট draft model আগে থেকে কয়েকটা টোকেন গেস করে, আর মূল (target) model সেগুলো প্যারালালি ভেরিফাই করে।

Attention mechanism অপ্টিমাইজ করার জন্য KV cache ব্যবহার হয়, যাতে আগের টোকেনের key-value ভেক্টর বারবার কম্পিউট করতে না হয়। তবে লম্বা context বা বড় batch size-এ এই cache অনেক মেমোরি খেয়ে ফেলতে পারে, তাই multi-query attention, grouped-query attention, আর FlashAttention-এর মতো kernel optimization দরকার হয়।

blocks.html: বাসের উপমা: প্রতিটা রিকোয়েস্ট আলাদা গাড়িতে পাঠানোর বদলে, batching হলো সবাইকে একসাথে একটা বাসে তোলা — এতে খরচ কমে, তবে বাস ছাড়তে একটু দেরি হতে পারে। Continuous batching-এ বাস থেকে একজন নামলেই আরেকজন উঠে যায়, তাই বাসটা সবসময় প্রায় ভরা থাকে।

bangla.html: সার্ভিস লেভেলে আরও টেকনিক আছে: prefill আর decode আলাদা মেশিনে চালানো, বারবার ব্যবহৃত প্রম্পট অংশ cache করে রাখা (prompt caching), আর বড় মডেলকে একাধিক GPU-তে ভাগ করে চালানো (tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, replica parallelism)। এসব টেকনিক সাধারণত মডেলের আউটপুট কোয়ালিটি না বদলে শুধু speed আর cost ঠিক করার চেষ্টা করে।

bn.title: AI ইঞ্জিনিয়ারিং আর্কিটেকচার এবং ইউজার ফিডব্যাক
bn.sub: একটা সিঙ্গেল মডেল কলের অ্যাপ কীভাবে ধাপে ধাপে ফুল প্ল্যাটফর্ম হয়ে ওঠে, আর ইউজাররা কীভাবে একে উন্নত হতে শেখায়

body.html: From one model call to a full platform

The simplest possible AI application is just a query sent to a model API and a response returned to the user — no context, no safety checks, no optimization. Real production systems grow out of this baseline one layer at a time, each layer added to solve a specific pain point rather than out of a desire for complexity.

items: Enhance context — give the model access to external data and tools so it has what it needs to answer well.
Put in guardrails — protect the system and the user from bad inputs and bad outputs.
Add a model router and gateway — manage multiple models, pipelines, and access control.
Reduce latency with caches — reuse previous work instead of recomputing it.
Add agent patterns — allow loops, branching, and write actions for more capable behavior.

body.html: Monitoring and observability, and the orchestration layer that chains every component together, sit above all five steps rather than being one more step in the sequence.
Context construction and guardrails

Context construction is essentially feature engineering for foundation models: retrieval (text, image, tabular) and tool use (web search, SQL, APIs) feed the model the information it needs for a specific query. Because this step shapes output quality so directly, almost every model API provider now supports some form of it, though providers differ in document limits, retrieval algorithms, and tool-calling modes.

Guardrails fall into two groups. Input guardrails defend against leaking private data to external APIs (an employee pasting secrets into a prompt, a tool pulling sensitive records into context) and against prompt attacks. A common pattern is to mask sensitive data with a placeholder like [PHONE NUMBER] before the call, then unmask it afterward using a reversible map. Output guardrails catch failures after generation — malformatted responses, hallucinations, toxic or private content, and brand-risk answers — and decide the policy for handling them: block, retry, or route to a human.

blocks.html: Guardrails trade safety for latency: every check adds a round trip or a scoring pass, and output guardrails get harder in streaming mode because tokens may reach the user before the full response can be evaluated. A system can also be too safe — tracking the false refusal rate matters as much as tracking security failures.

body.html: Model router and gateway

A router uses an intent classifier to send each query to the right place — a cheap model for simple questions, a specialized model for billing, a human for anything the classifier can't handle. Routers also catch out-of-scope requests before an expensive model call is made, and can ask for clarification when a query is ambiguous. They are usually small, fast, and cheap on purpose, since they sit in front of every single request.

A gateway is a unified interface between an application and every model it uses, self-hosted or third-party. Instead of distributing provider API keys across every application, a gateway centralizes access control, usage monitoring, cost limits, and fallback logic (retrying or switching providers when a call fails or hits a rate limit). Since every request already passes through it, a gateway is also a natural place to add load balancing, logging, caching, and guardrails.
Reducing latency with caches

Two system-level caching strategies are common. Exact caching stores results keyed to an identical query (or an identical retrieval request) and reuses them only on an exact match — useful for repeated multi-step queries, with an eviction policy such as LRU or LFU to bound cache size. Semantic caching reuses a cached answer for a query that is only similar, not identical, by comparing embeddings against a similarity threshold.

rows: Caching a response that was actually personalized to one user, then serving it to someone else
A bad threshold returns a wrong answer that looks plausible; adds vector-search cost

body.html: Agent patterns and write actions

Once an architecture supports loops, parallel execution, and conditional branching, it crosses into agentic territory: a model can decide its first answer was incomplete, trigger another retrieval, and feed the new context back into itself or a different model. The architecture can go one step further by allowing write actions — sending an email, placing an order, updating a database — which make the system far more capable but also far riskier, since a mistake is no longer just a bad answer but a real-world side effect.
Monitoring and observability

Monitoring tracks a system's outputs; observability goes further, assuming that internal state can be inferred from logs and metrics without shipping new code just to diagnose a problem. Three DevOps-derived metrics help judge how observable a system is: MTTD (mean time to detection), MTTR (mean time to response), and CFR (change failure rate, the share of deployments that need a fix or rollback).

items: Metrics should be designed around specific failure modes — format failures, hallucination signals, toxicity, refusal rate, and cost/latency figures like TTFT, TPOT, and tokens per request.
Logs are an append-only record of events; the common advice is to log everything, since it's rarely obvious in advance what you'll need to debug later.
Traces reconstruct a single request's full path — retrieval, tool calls, model calls, timing, cost — so a failure can be pinpointed to the exact step that went wrong.

body.html: A system should also be watched for drift: an unnoticed change to the system prompt, users gradually adapting how they phrase requests, or the underlying model silently changing behind an unchanged API.
AI pipeline orchestration

An orchestrator wires all the components together in two steps: component definition (declaring the models, data sources, and tools available) and chaining (specifying the order of operations — process query, retrieve, build the prompt, generate, evaluate, then return to the user or escalate to a human). Where latency is tight, independent steps such as routing and PII redaction should run in parallel rather than in sequence. Adopting a heavy orchestration framework early can hide details you still need to understand about your own system, so starting without one is often the better default.
Extracting conversational feedback

Feedback is explicit (thumbs up/down, star ratings, a direct yes/no) or implicit (inferred from what a user does). Conversational interfaces make implicit feedback unusually rich: a user's follow-up message itself signals success or failure. Early termination, a correction starting with "No, I meant...", regenerating a response, editing the output directly, and simply expressing frustration are all natural language signals that can be tracked in production, and can serve evaluation, model development, and personalization.
Feedback design

Feedback should be collectible throughout the user journey without interrupting it: during onboarding (calibrating to a new user), right after a failure (letting the user downvote, regenerate, or correct), and when the model itself has low confidence (showing two candidate outputs and letting the user pick, as with comparative evaluation). Good feedback design makes giving feedback nearly free — Midjourney's upscale/variation/regenerate buttons and GitHub Copilot's accept-or-keep-typing flow are both cited as examples that collect signal without asking users to do anything extra.
Feedback limitations

User feedback is valuable but biased and incomplete. Leniency bias pushes ratings upward when negative feedback feels like extra work or conflict. Position bias favors whichever option is shown first. Preference bias rewards length or recency over actual correctness. Feedback is also only ever collected on what the system already chose to show, which can produce a degenerate feedback loop: popular outputs get shown more, get more clicks, and get reinforced further, while anything not shown never gets a chance to prove itself — the mechanism behind popularity bias and filter bubbles. Training a model directly on user feedback can also push it toward sycophancy, optimizing for what users want to hear rather than what is accurate.

layman.html: Think of building an AI app like building a house. You start with four walls and a roof — just send the question to the model and show the answer. Then, because real problems come up, you add plumbing (giving the model outside information like documents or search results), locks on the doors (guardrails that block bad requests or bad answers), a reception desk (a router that sends different questions to different rooms), and a pantry (caching, so you don't cook the same meal twice).

blocks.html: Restaurant analogy: monitoring is like a manager watching the dining room — are plates coming back untouched, are customers waiting too long, are any dishes making people sick? Logs and traces are the kitchen's ticket system: when something goes wrong, you can walk back through exactly which station touched the order and when.

layman.html: The second half of this chapter is about listening to customers. Every time a user corrects the AI, stops it mid-answer, regenerates a response, or just says "that's wrong," they are quietly teaching the system what good and bad look like. The trick is collecting that feedback without being annoying about it — the best designs (like an image generator letting you simply pick your favorite of four pictures) get useful signal for free.

items: Not all feedback is honest or fair: people rate things kinder than they feel, click the first option out of habit, or prefer long answers even when a short one was more correct.
If you only ever show your most popular answers, they get more clicks and look even more popular — new, possibly better answers never get a chance. This is the trap called a degenerate feedback loop.

bangla.html: একটা AI অ্যাপ সবচেয়ে সহজ অবস্থায় শুধু একটা model API-তে query পাঠায় আর response ফেরত দেয় — কোনো context, guardrail বা optimization ছাড়াই। প্রোডাকশনে গিয়ে এই সহজ কাঠামোর উপর ধাপে ধাপে ০৫টা স্তর যোগ হয়: context enhance করা, guardrails বসানো, router আর gateway যোগ করা, caching দিয়ে latency কমানো, আর agent pattern যোগ করে জটিল কাজ করানো।

Context construction হলো foundation model-এর জন্য ফিচার ইঞ্জিনিয়ারিং-এর মতো — retrieval আর tool use দিয়ে মডেলকে উত্তর দেয়ার জন্য দরকারি তথ্য দেওয়া হয়। Guardrails দুই ধরনের: input guardrail লিক হওয়া sensitive তথ্য আর prompt attack ঠেকায় (যেমন ফোন নম্বর [PHONE NUMBER] দিয়ে মাস্ক করে পরে আনমাস্ক করা), আর output guardrail hallucination, toxic content, বা malformatted output ধরে ফেলে।

Router একটা intent classifier দিয়ে ঠিক করে কোন query কোথায় যাবে — সস্তা মডেল না বিশেষায়িত মডেল, নাকি মানুষ অপারেটর। Gateway সব মডেলের (self-hosted বা third-party) জন্য একটা একক API দেয়, যাতে access control, cost management আর fallback (একটা provider fail করলে অন্যটায় যাওয়া) কেন্দ্রীয়ভাবে করা যায়।

items: Exact caching: হুবহু একই query-র জন্য আগের উত্তর রিইউজ করা।
Semantic caching: embedding মিল থাকলে কাছাকাছি অর্থের query-র জন্যও cache রিইউজ করা, তবে threshold ভুল হলে ভুল উত্তর আসার ঝুঁকি থাকে।

bangla.html: Agent pattern দিয়ে সিস্টেম loop চালাতে পারে (উত্তর যথেষ্ট না হলে আবার retrieval করে নিজেকে ফিডব্যাক দেওয়া), আর write action (ইমেইল পাঠানো, অর্ডার বসানো) যোগ করলে সিস্টেম অনেক বেশি কার্যকর কিন্তু ঝুঁকিপূর্ণও হয়ে যায়। Monitoring আর observability-তে metrics, logs, আর traces — এই তিনটা মিলিয়ে বোঝা যায় সিস্টেম কোথায় ভেঙেছে, আর orchestration সব component একসাথে চেইন করে দেয়।

blocks.html: উপমা: ইউজার যখন AI-কে বলে "না, আমি এটা বলিনি" বা মাঝপথে থামিয়ে দেয়, সেটাও একধরনের ফিডব্যাক — যেমন রেস্টুরেন্টে প্লেট অর্ধেক খাওয়া অবস্থায় ফেরত গেলে বোঝা যায় রান্না ভালো হয়নি।

bangla.html: Feedback explicit (thumbs up/down, star rating) বা implicit (ইউজারের আচরণ থেকে বোঝা) হতে পারে। ভালো feedback design হলো সেটা যা ইউজারের কাজে বাধা না দিয়ে সিগন্যাল সংগ্রহ করে — যেমন Midjourney-তে একটা ছবি upscale করার বাটন চাপাই বলে দেয় কোনটা পছন্দ হয়েছে।

blocks.html: তবে feedback-এ bias থাকে: leniency bias (মানুষ বেশি খারাপ রেটিং দিতে অস্বস্তি বোধ করে), position bias (প্রথম অপশনেই বেশি ক্লিক পড়ে), আর degenerate feedback loop — যেখানে জনপ্রিয় উত্তরই বারবার দেখানো হয়, তাই সেটাই আরও বেশি ক্লিক পায়, আর নতুন ভালো উত্তর কখনো সুযোগই পায় না।

Chip Huyen's blog — ongoing writing on AI engineering, evaluation, and ML systems
AI Engineering book — companion resources repository

en.q: According to the book, what mainly separates AI engineering from traditional ML engineering?
options: AI engineering never involves writing any code
AI engineering only applies to image models
AI engineering adapts an already-trained foundation model instead of training one from scratch
AI engineering does not need any evaluation
en.why: Foundation models shift the work from training models to adapting and evaluating already-trained ones — prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning instead of building a model from zero.

bn.q: বই অনুযায়ী, AI engineering আর সাধারণ ML engineering-এর মূল পার্থক্য কী?
options: AI engineering-এ কোনো কোড লেখা লাগে না
AI engineering শুধু ইমেজ মডেলের জন্য প্রযোজ্য
AI engineering আগে থেকে ট্রেইন করা একটা foundation model-কে adapt করে, শূন্য থেকে ট্রেইন করে না
AI engineering-এ কোনো evaluation লাগে না
bn.why: Foundation model থাকার কারণে কাজটা হয়ে যায় prompting, RAG, আর fine-tuning দিয়ে আগের মডেলকে adapt করা — শূন্য থেকে মডেল বানানো নয়।

en.q: Using a strong AI model as a judge to score another model's output is a real evaluation technique covered in the book, even though it has known limitations.
en.why: "AI as a judge" is covered as a practical, scalable evaluation method, alongside its limitations such as judge bias and inconsistency.

bn.q: একটা শক্তিশালী AI মডেলকে বিচারক (judge) হিসেবে ব্যবহার করে আরেকটা মডেলের আউটপুট স্কোর করা — এটা বইয়ে আলোচিত একটা বাস্তব evaluation পদ্ধতি, যদিও এর কিছু সীমাবদ্ধতা আছে।
bn.why: "AI as a judge" পদ্ধতিটা বইয়ে একটা practical, স্কেলেবল evaluation কৌশল হিসেবে আলোচিত হয়েছে, সাথে এর সীমাবদ্ধতাও (যেমন judge bias, অসামঞ্জস্যতা) দেখানো হয়েছে।

en.q: Per the chapter on finetuning, what is the main reason a team might choose RAG over finetuning first?
options: RAG always produces a smaller model file
RAG adds fresh or private knowledge without retraining the model, while finetuning changes the model's behavior/skills
Finetuning cannot run on a GPU
RAG removes the need for evaluation entirely
en.why: RAG is generally the first lever for giving a model missing or up-to-date knowledge; finetuning is better suited to changing behavior, format, or specialized skills.

bn.q: ফাইন-টিউনিং চ্যাপ্টার অনুযায়ী, ফাইন-টিউনিংয়ের আগে RAG বেছে নেওয়ার মূল কারণ কী?
options: RAG সবসময় ছোট মডেল ফাইল তৈরি করে
RAG মডেলকে রিট্রেইন না করেই নতুন বা প্রাইভেট তথ্য যোগ করে, আর ফাইন-টিউনিং মডেলের আচরণ/দক্ষতা পাল্টায়
ফাইন-টিউনিং GPU-তে চালানো যায় না
RAG ব্যবহার করলে কোনো evaluation লাগে না
bn.why: মডেলের মিসিং বা আপ-টু-ডেট তথ্যের সমস্যা সমাধানে সাধারণত RAG-ই প্রথম পদক্ষেপ; আচরণ, ফরম্যাট বা বিশেষ দক্ষতা পাল্টাতে ফাইন-টিউনিং বেশি উপযোগী।

en.q: According to the inference optimization chapter, making a model faster always requires buying more powerful hardware.
en.why: The book covers many software-level optimizations — quantization, speculative decoding, better batching, prompt caching — that speed up inference without new hardware.

bn.q: ইনফারেন্স অপ্টিমাইজেশন চ্যাপ্টার অনুযায়ী, মডেলকে দ্রুত চালাতে সবসময় আরও শক্তিশালী হার্ডওয়্যার কিনতে হয়।
bn.why: বইয়ে quantization, speculative decoding, ভালো batching, prompt caching-এর মতো অনেক সফটওয়্যার-লেভেল অপ্টিমাইজেশন আলোচিত হয়েছে, যেগুলো নতুন হার্ডওয়্যার ছাড়াই ইনফারেন্স দ্রুত করে।

en.q: In the final chapter on AI engineering architecture, what is the typical first step suggested for improving a basic prompt-only application?
options: Enhance context — e.g. add retrieval, so the model has relevant information to work with
Immediately deploy on 1,000 GPUs
Remove all guardrails for maximum speed
Stop collecting any user feedback
en.why: The architecture chapter builds up a system step by step, starting with enhancing context (e.g. RAG) before adding guardrails, routing, caching, and agent patterns.

bn.q: শেষ চ্যাপ্টারে (AI engineering architecture) একটা বেসিক prompt-only অ্যাপ্লিকেশন উন্নত করার প্রথম ধাপ হিসেবে সাধারণত কী বলা হয়েছে?
options: কনটেক্সট বাড়ানো — যেমন retrieval যোগ করা, যাতে মডেল প্রাসঙ্গিক তথ্য দিয়ে কাজ করতে পারে
সাথে সাথে ১,০০০টা GPU-তে ডিপ্লয় করা
সর্বোচ্চ গতির জন্য সব গার্ডরেল সরিয়ে ফেলা
ইউজার ফিডব্যাক সংগ্রহ বন্ধ করে দেওয়া
bn.why: আর্কিটেকচার চ্যাপ্টারে ধাপে ধাপে সিস্টেম তৈরির কথা বলা হয়েছে, যেখানে প্রথমে কনটেক্সট বাড়ানো (যেমন RAG), তারপর গার্ডরেল, রাউটিং, ক্যাশিং, আর এজেন্ট প্যাটার্ন যোগ করা হয়।
